problem: Existing testing/fuzzing methods for embodied (VLN) agents are system-level: they only detect task failures and cannot say which capability (perception, memory, planning, decision) caused them, especially with error propagation over long trajectories.
motivation: Developers need interpretable, capability-level diagnoses to fix embodied agents in safety-critical uses. Capabilities are interdependent and errors cascade over time, so pinpointing the initial failure-inducing error and using it to guide test generation is valuable.
key_idea: Fuzz VLN agents with LLM-generated instruction test cases guided by feedback that combines task-failure and capability-level error, where per-capability oracles plus counterfactual intervention attribute each failure to its earliest failure-inducing capability error.
insight: Attributing failures to capabilities via oracle-based counterfactual replacement gives a richer guidance signal than system-level outcomes: ablating either failure-oriented (FOF) or capability-oriented (COF) feedback, or all feedback, reduces failures found, and FOF and COF matter about equally. The adaptive weight lambda balances coverage across capabilities. Oracle outputs replacing erroneous capability outputs repair 81-97% of failures, supporting oracle fidelity, and upstream capabilities are harder to repair than decision.
method: Adaptive test case generation: an LLM combines HM3D room/object annotations into navigation instructions (test cases); seeds are selected with probability proportional to feedback score in a fuzzing loop.

Mild vs aggressive mutation: high-feedback seeds get mild mutation (change the destination object within the same room), low-feedback seeds get aggressive mutation (change the target room); the choice is probabilistic via a rank-normalized p_m.

Capability oracles: expert signals (greedy shortest-path navigator, RAM image annotator) define errors. Perception uses LLM-judged annotation similarity plus IoU; memory uses LLM similarity between memory description and GT history annotations; planning uses 1-nDTW against the expert trajectory; decision uses mismatch between action and planned action.

Counterfactual failure attribution: for each detected error (C_x,t) in a failed trajectory, replace the agent output with the oracle output and re-roll out; if it turns into success it is failure-inducing, and the earliest such error is the failure-source capability.

Feedback score: F = F^f (failure-oriented) + lambda^{C_x} * F^c (normalized oracle error at the source step); lambda is the mean failure count over capabilities divided by the count for the source capability, to balance capability coverage.

setting.backbone: Test targets: ApexNav, MGDM, Mem2Ego (VLN/navigation agents under test); an LLM is used for instruction generation/mutation and for the perception/memory oracle similarity (model not named in the text)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB from three directions (forward, left, right)
setting.action_space: low-level discrete: Move Forward, Turn Left, Turn Right, Stop
setting.privileged: expert models for oracles: global-map greedy shortest-path navigator and RAM annotator for GT detections; counterfactual oracle output substitution

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark results (SR/SPL etc.). Metrics are counts of discovered failure cases (main comparison only in a figure), per-capability failure counts (Table 2), and repair rates (Table 3); none are standard benchmark numbers.
results: The method finds the most failure cases, 23.34%–33.70% more than the best baseline (VLATest), across ApexNav, MGDM and Mem2Ego. With the OA plug-in added to baselines it still finds the most failures per capability (e.g., ApexNav perception 72.2 vs 51.8 for VLATest+OA). Oracle-based repair rates are 81.30%–96.69%.
limitations: Requires an expert model (near-optimal route, semantic grounding) to build oracles; without one, extra supervision is needed.
Evaluated only in simulation (Habitat 3/HM3D); transfer to the physical world is non-trivial.
Only three target agents and four capabilities; the oracles rely on LLM judgement, and the single-source attribution assumes the earliest failure-inducing error is decisive.
